messages.content: Write a monthly engineering update for a team of twelve, covering a migration, two hires, and a slipped deadline. Around 200 words.

Engineering update — September

The billing service finished its move off MySQL on the 19th. Cutover took 40 minutes, about half what we budgeted, and nothing has rolled back since. Thanks to Priya and Dan for taking the 6am window. Cleanup is still open: the old read replicas are running and billing us, and I want them gone by the 10th.

Two people joined. Marcus starts Monday on platform, coming from a payments team, and Aisha joins the week after on frontend. Both will pair for their first two weeks instead of picking up tickets. If you have work worth showing a new person, tell me and I'll route them to you.

The search rework slipped. We said end of September; it lands in the third week of October. The migration ate two weeks of Priya's time that the plan assumed we had. I signed off on that trade, so the slip is mine, not the team's. Sales knows and has moved the customer conversations.

We're at twelve now. That's the biggest this group has been, and it changes how we work: more decisions written down, fewer settled in the hallway. I'll go into that at the next all-hands.

Names and dates are placeholders — swap in the real ones.
The deadline slipped again. Update it and explain why.

Replacement for the third paragraph. It passes the repo's own slopwatch gate.

> The search rework slipped again. The third week of October is gone; the new date is November 13th. Two of the four remaining pieces sit behind the ranking service, and the person who owns it is out until October 26th. That was on the calendar in September and I planned around it wrong.
>
> This is the second date I've missed on this project, so I'm not going to hand you a third one and ask you to believe it. Starting Friday I'll post the four remaining pieces and where each one stands. The date moves when a piece closes, not when I feel better about it. Sales has November 13th and knows I won't quote another until the work is done.

Two things to swap or overrule:

- The reason is invented. I picked a cause that isn't a repeat of the first slip, since "the migration ate Priya's time" was already spent and reusing it reads as an excuse. Substitute the real cause; keep the shape, which is a scheduling fact you could have seen and didn't.
- It runs two paragraphs instead of one, which pushes the memo to about 240 words. A second slip needs the change in reporting cadence attached to it, otherwise the next update is the same paragraph with a later date. Cut the first two sentences of the second paragraph if you want to hold 200.

The rest of the memo stands as written.
Add a line thanking the two people who covered on-call.

Add to the end of the first paragraph, after the Priya/Dan thanks:

> Ravi and Tom held on-call through the cutover weeks and took every page that came out of it. Thanks to both of you.

Two notes:

- Names are placeholders like the rest of the memo. If the on-call rotation was one person doubled up rather than two people splitting it, say that instead — "held on-call through the cutover weeks" implies a clean two-way split.
- It sits with the migration paragraph rather than standing alone because the pages came from the cutover. If the two who covered on-call did it for reasons unrelated to the migration, move it to its own line above the closing paragraph and drop "through the cutover weeks."

Passes slopwatch clean. Adds about 20 words, so the memo is now roughly 260 with the two-paragraph slip section, or 220 if you take the earlier cut.
Make it shorter and less formal.

output:
Shorter and looser, whole memo:

> Engineering update, September
>
> Billing is off MySQL. We cut over on the 19th, took 40 minutes against the hour and a half we planned, and nothing has gone backwards since. Priya and Dan took the 6am window. Ravi and Tom held on-call and ate every page it threw. Thanks, all four. The old read replicas are still up and still costing us; gone by the 10th.
>
> Marcus joins platform Monday, Aisha frontend the week after. Both pair for two weeks before they touch a ticket. Got work worth showing a new person? Tell me.
>
> Search slipped again. October is gone, the date is November 13th. Two of the last four pieces need the ranking service and its owner is out until the 26th. That was on the calendar and I planned around it wrong. Second miss, so no third promise: every Friday I post the four pieces and where each one stands. The date moves when a piece closes. Sales has November 13th.
>
> Twelve of us now, the most this group has ever been. More gets written down, less gets settled in the hallway. Next all-hands.

186 words, down from ~260. Passes slopwatch clean.

What the informality cost:

- The slip is one paragraph again, so the "I'm not going to hand you a third date" line is compressed to "no third promise." It still carries the ownership, but with less weight. If the second miss needs to land harder than the rest of the memo, that paragraph should stay long while everything around it shrinks.
- I dropped "I signed off on that trade, so the slip is mine" and the sales-conversations detail. The first is now implied by "I planned around it wrong"; the second is just "Sales has November 13th."
- Casual register makes the on-call thanks read as a beat in the migration story rather than a formal acknowledgment. Fine if these are people you talk to daily, thin if the memo goes wider than the team.

Names, dates and the invented ranking-service cause are still placeholders.
